Bessel and Hankel functions

Source: R/bessel.R
bessel-functions.Rd

Cylindrical Bessel functions of real order and real or complex argument, with scipy.special's names and argument order: order first, argument second. Base R's besselJ() and siblings take them the other way round and accept only real arguments.

Usage

sc_jv(v, z)

sc_yv(v, z)

sc_iv(v, z)

sc_kv(v, z)

sc_jve(v, z)

sc_yve(v, z)

sc_ive(v, z)

sc_kve(v, z)

sc_hankel1(v, z)

sc_hankel2(v, z)

sc_hankel1e(v, z)

sc_hankel2e(v, z)

sc_j0(x)

sc_j1(x)

sc_y0(x)

sc_y1(x)

sc_i0(x)

sc_i0e(x)

sc_i1(x)

sc_i1e(x)

sc_k0(x)

sc_k0e(x)

sc_k1(x)

sc_k1e(x)

Arguments

v

Numeric vector of orders.

z

Numeric or complex vector of arguments.

x

Numeric vector.

Value

A double vector, or a complex vector for complex z (always for the Hankel functions).

Details

  • sc_jv(), sc_yv(), sc_iv(), sc_kv(): \(J_v(z)\), \(Y_v(z)\), \(I_v(z)\), \(K_v(z)\). Base R: besselJ(z, v) and so on.

  • sc_jve(), sc_yve(), sc_ive(), sc_kve(): the exponentially scaled forms, \(J_v(z) e^{-|\Im z|}\), \(Y_v(z) e^{-|\Im z|}\), \(I_v(z) e^{-|\Re z|}\) and \(K_v(z) e^z\). Base R: the expon.scaled = TRUE forms of besselI() and besselK().

  • sc_hankel1(), sc_hankel2(): \(H^{(1)}_v(z) = J_v(z) + i Y_v(z)\) and \(H^{(2)}_v(z)\); sc_hankel1e(), sc_hankel2e() scale them by \(e^{\mp iz}\). SciPy defines them for complex z only, so real input is treated as complex and the result is always complex.

  • sc_j0(), sc_j1(), sc_y0(), sc_y1(), sc_i0(), sc_i0e(), sc_i1(), sc_i1e(), sc_k0(), sc_k0e(), sc_k1(), sc_k1e(): orders 0 and 1 for real x, faster than the general functions.

A complex z takes the complex path and returns complex; a real z stays real, so sc_jv(0.5, -1) is NaN while sc_jv(0.5, -1+0i) is complex, as in SciPy. The order v must be real. Arguments are recycled, NA gives NA, and the result takes its dimensions, or else its names, from the arguments as base R arithmetic does; see sc_seterr() for the conditions the kernels raise.

Windows

R on Windows is built with Rtools, whose C library (mingw-w64 v11) evaluates sin() and cos() inaccurately for arguments beyond about 1e5, as base R's own sin() shows there. Arguments that large are correspondingly inaccurate on Windows only.

Branch cuts

For complex z, as in SciPy: \(J_v\) and \(I_v\) are entire in z for a whole order v, and otherwise have a branch cut on the negative real axis; \(Y_v\), \(K_v\) and the Hankel functions have that cut for every order.

Other packages

In gsl, for real arguments, in SciPy's order: bessel_Jnu(nu, x), bessel_Ynu(), bessel_Inu(), bessel_Knu(), the scaled bessel_Inu_scaled() and bessel_Knu_scaled(), and bessel_J0() to bessel_K1_scaled(). In Bessel, for complex arguments, in base R's order: BesselJ(z, nu), BesselY(), BesselI(), BesselK() and BesselH(m, z, nu).

See also

https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/special.html#bessel-functions

Examples

sc_jv(c(0, 1, 2.5), 3)
#> [1] -0.260052  0.339059  0.412710
sc_jv(0.5, -1)
#> [1] NaN
sc_jv(0.5, -1 + 0i)
#> [1] 5.551115e-17+0.6713967i
sc_kve(1, 50)
#> [1] 0.1785666
sc_hankel1(0, 2)
#> [1] 0.2238908+0.5103757i
sc_j0(c(0, 2.405))
#> [1]  1.0000e+00 -9.0558e-05
